## Introduction

The Inference pages share one **known-truth** case study. We pick parameter
values, simulate *pseudo-observed* data there, and check whether a method
recovers them. Run this kind of recovery test before pointing a method at field
data.

This page builds the case study and covers the first of the three steps in
@hartig2011: **aggregation**, the choice of summary statistics. It ends with
everything a method page needs: the pseudo-observed data, 200 simulations from
the prior, and the z-score of each statistic. Method pages start from the
middle with one call, `case.known_truth_study().load(...)`, which reuses the
runs this page made.

The workflow is the same for any model, so joshpy runs it:
`KnownTruthStudy` (experimental, in `joshpy.inference`). The case study
supplies only what is specific to ForeverTree: the model, how a field study
would observe it, and the candidate statistics.

::: {.callout-note}
## Runtime

The first render runs about 250 simulations of a small model (roughly 15
minutes on a laptop, one simulation at a time). They are stored in the shared
registry `forevertree.duckdb`, so later pages reuse them instead of
re-simulating.
:::

The case study's code lives in one module,
`examples/sbi_forevertree/forevertree_case.py`. The docs pages and the
command-line example `run_abc.py` both import it:

```{python}
import sys

sys.path.insert(0, "../../examples/sbi_forevertree")
import forevertree_case as case
import pandas as pd

from joshpy.cli import JoshCLI
from joshpy.jar import JarMode
from joshpy.registry import RunRegistry

registry = RunRegistry("forevertree.duckdb")  # shared by the Inference pages
cli = JoshCLI(josh_jar=JarMode.DEV)
```

## The Model

We use the ForeverTree model from the Josh paper: ten trees per 16 km cell, on
a grid of 63 cells, grow each year by up to `maxNewGrowth`, scaled by a
temperature response and a precipitation response. Drought slows growth, and
`minPrecipImpactPct` sets how much: at 0% a dry year halts growth, at 100%
drought has no effect.

The model is **stochastic**: each tree's growth each year is multiplied by a
draw from a normal distribution with mean 100% and standard deviation 5%. Each
run is therefore one draw from a distribution of outputs,
$p(D_\text{sim} \mid \theta)$, that we can sample but can't write down. That is
why the likelihood is intractable and has to be approximated
[@hartig2011, fig. 2].

| Parameter | Meaning | Prior | Truth |
|-----------|---------|-------|-------|
| `maxNewGrowth` | Maximum height gain per year | Uniform, 0.2 to 2.0 m | 1.0 m |
| `minPrecipImpactPct` | Growth retained in the driest years | Uniform, 0 to 100% | 40% |

## Put `{run_hash}` in the export path

`SbiStrategy` runs each batch of parameter sets **before** loading any of them,
so every run needs its own output file:

```josh
exportFiles.patch = "file:///tmp/forevertree_abc_{run_hash}_{replicate}.csv"
```

Without `{run_hash}` (or `{label}`), every run in a batch would write the same
CSV, so joshpy refuses such a batch with an error.
:::

## The Pseudo-Observed Data: a Survey

Field data are never as complete as a simulation's output. A monitoring program
measures a fixed set of sites, each with error. To mirror that, the
pseudo-observed data are a **survey**:

- the final-year mean tree height of **8 fixed cells**, spread across the
  climate gradient;
- each **measured with error**: normal, with a standard deviation of
  0.25 m.

The measurement error is part of the model. Every cell exports a measured height
next to its true mean height:

```josh
export.measuredHeight.step =
  mean(ForeverTree.height)
  + sample normal with mean of 0 m std of 0.25 m
```

Each run therefore carries its own measurement error, drawn by Josh like the
growth noise and stored in the registry with the rest of the run's output. The
case study then keeps only the surveyed cells. Simulating the observer along
with the system is the *virtual ecologist* approach [@zurell2010]. Every cell is
exported, so the choice of surveyed cells can change without re-simulating. A
different error model means editing the model, which changes every `run_hash`,
so every run is simulated again.

The same survey is applied to the truth and to every simulation. Statistics
must be computed the same way for observed and simulated data, and simulating
the survey makes its error part of the variability that comes from within the
model. The tolerance $\varepsilon$ then carries only the approximation error.
The alternative is to leave the survey unsimulated and size $\varepsilon$ to the
observation error, which makes ABC exact for the model plus that error model
[@wilkinson2013].

The survey, from the model's output to measured heights:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
case.show_source(case.final_heights, case.observe)
```

The truth run gets its own seed (`seed=3`), so the page is reproducible. The
simulations used for inference leave `seed` unset, so each draws its own noise,
in growth and in measurement, as independent realizations of a stochastic model
should.

## Defining the Study

Everything after the survey is the same for any model. `KnownTruthStudy` takes
the model, the prior, the truth and the two functions specific to ForeverTree,
`observe` above and `statistics` below. It runs the truth and the prior
simulations, and the comparisons that follow, reusing every run the registry
already holds. This is the whole ForeverTree definition:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
case.show_source(case.known_truth_study)
```

For another model, write its `observe` and `statistics`, and the rest of this
page applies unchanged. The [Architecture](../architecture.qmd#knowntruthstudy)
page shows how the study fits with the rest of joshpy.

```{python}
study = case.known_truth_study().load(registry, cli)
study.truth_data.round(2)
```

`load` runs the truth and 200 prior simulations, unless the registry already
holds them. `study.truth_data` is the pseudo-observed survey: each site's true
final-year height and its measured value.

## Simulating the Prior

Every ABC method starts by simulating parameter sets drawn from the prior.
`load` draws 200 with sbi's rejection ABC (`method="mcabc"`) set to keep every
draw (`quantile=1.0`), which makes it a plain prior simulation. With the same
sbi seed, a later search's first draws are these same parameter sets, so it
reuses these runs.

```{python}
study.reference.drop(columns="run_hash").describe().loc[["count", "mean", "std", "min", "max"]].round(3)
```

Each row of `study.reference` holds one simulation's parameters and its
candidate statistics: the **reference table** of ABC [@csillery2012]. The
registry holds every run's full output, so statistics we haven't thought of yet
can be computed later without re-simulating.

## Choosing Summary Statistics

Summary statistics are where knowledge of the system enters [@hartig2011]. A
good set pins down every parameter and is computed the same way for observed and
simulated data. It also stays small: each statistic added makes a close match
rarer and forces a larger tolerance.

### The candidates

For the measured heights $y_1, \dots, y_n$ of the $n = 8$ surveyed cells, four
candidates come to mind:

| Statistic | Definition | Describes |
|-----------|------------|-----------|
| Mean | $\bar{y} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} y_i$ | How tall the trees are |
| SD | $s = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n-1} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - \bar{y})^2}$ | How much heights differ between sites |
| Variance | $s^2$ | The same, squared |
| CV | $s / \bar{y}$ | How much heights differ between sites, relative to their mean |

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
case.show_source(case.statistics)
```

Plotting each candidate against each parameter, over the prior simulations,
shows what each one can tell us. ρ is the Spearman rank correlation.

```{python}
#| label: fig-candidates
#| fig-cap: "Candidate statistics of the survey against each parameter, over 200 prior simulations. The orange dashed line is the statistic's pseudo-observed value; the black line is the parameter's true value. The mean moves with both parameters; the CV moves with drought sensitivity (minPrecipImpactPct) and hardly at all with growth."
case.plot_candidates(study)
```

```{python}
study.correlations().rename(index=case.LABELS).round(2)
```

### Choosing among them

No recipe guarantees sufficient statistics, but a process helps:

1. **Start from patterns.** Candidates come from what the model is meant to
   reproduce and what a field study can measure. Pattern-oriented modelling
   calls these *patterns*, and combining patterns observed at different scales
   is a recognized way to approach sufficiency [@grimm2005; @hartig2011]. Here
   they are the level of the surveyed heights and their spread across the
   climate gradient.
2. **Keep statistics that move with the parameters.** A statistic that is flat
   against every parameter in @fig-candidates carries no information about
   them.
3. **Look for a set that separates the parameters.** Ideally each parameter has
   a statistic that tracks it, so that no two parameter combinations give the
   same statistics. Where parameters can trade off against each other, the
   posterior follows a ridge, a case of equifinality [@beven2006].
4. **Drop redundant statistics, and choose their form.** Statistics computed
   from each other carry the same information, but the form decides how the
   distance combines them (the example below).
5. **Compare signal with noise.** A statistic's spread between replicates at one
   parameter value should be small next to its spread across the prior. The
   [replicate study](#what-the-likelihood-approximation-compares) below checks
   this.
6. **Test for sufficiency on simulated data.** A statistic is *sufficient* if it
   keeps all the information in the data that is relevant to the parameters,
   so that $p(\theta \mid S_\text{obs}) = p(\theta \mid D_\text{obs})$. Minimal
   sufficiency is desirable but not required [@hartig2011]. The figure shows that
   mean and CV are *informative*, which is weaker, and the survey discards most
   cells and every year before the last. Sufficiency usually has to be tested on
   artificial data [@hartig2011]; the [SMC-ABC page](smc-abc.qmd) does that by dropping the CV.

There are automatic, model-agnostic alternatives: add statistics one at a time
and keep those that change the posterior [@joyce2008], or construct one
statistic per parameter by regressing the parameters on many candidate features
over the prior simulations [@fearnhead2012]. @blum2013 compare such methods.

**Step 4 in practice: CV or variance?** The pairs (mean, variance) and
(mean, CV) carry the same information, since each can be computed from the
other. What differs is how a distance combines them, which matters because the
tolerance is not zero. ForeverTree is multiplicative in `maxNewGrowth`:

```josh
newGrowth.step = meta.maxNewGrowth * temperatureImpact * precipImpact * stochastic
```

So every cell's height scales with `maxNewGrowth`: the mean and the SD of the
surveyed heights scale with it, and the variance with its square. The CV
divides growth out and tracks drought sensitivity, which spreads wet and dry
cells apart. (A little dependence on growth remains, because the measurement
error is additive and weighs more when trees are short.) Mean and CV therefore
give roughly one statistic per parameter, as step 3 asks: the CV pins down
`minPrecipImpactPct`, and the mean then pins down `maxNewGrowth`. Mean and
variance mix both parameters in both statistics. ABC compares the mean and the
CV.

## Scaling: z-Scores

Most ABC methods compare statistics with a Euclidean distance. It adds up
squared differences, so a statistic with a larger spread would dominate: across
the prior, the mean height varies by metres and the CV by tenths. So each
statistic becomes a **z-score**, using its mean $\mu$ and standard deviation
$\sigma$ across the prior simulations:

$$
z(S) = \frac{S - \mu}{\sigma}
$$

Dividing by $\sigma$ puts every statistic on the same scale [@hartig2011;
@beaumont2002]. Subtracting $\mu$ changes nothing ABC uses, because it cancels
in every difference: $z(S_\text{sim}) - z(S_\text{obs}) = (S_\text{sim} -
S_\text{obs}) / \sigma$. It only centres the values, so a z-score reads as the
number of prior SDs above or below the average simulation. Distances and
tolerances on the Inference pages are in z-score units.

```{python}
pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "pseudo-observed": study.observed,
        "prior mean (μ)": study.center,
        "prior SD (σ)": study.scale,
        "pseudo-observed z-score": study.zscore(study.observed),
    }
).loc[case.STATISTICS].rename(index=case.LABELS).round(3)
```

## From Model Output to a Comparison

Here is the whole aggregation step for the truth run, and the comparison an ABC
method makes with it. First, the model's output reduces to $S_\text{obs}$:

```{python}
#| label: fig-observation
#| fig-cap: "From model output to S_obs, for the pseudo-observed run. (1) Final-year height of all 63 cells; outlined cells are surveyed. (2) The survey records each site's height with the measurement error the model drew. (3) The eight measured heights reduce to a mean and a CV, which together are S_obs."
case.plot_observation(study, registry)
```

Every prior simulation goes through the same three steps and becomes one point
with its own mean and CV. An ABC method compares each point with $S_\text{obs}$
and accepts the simulations within a tolerance $\varepsilon$. For illustration,
$\varepsilon$ is set so that the closest 10% of the prior simulations fall
within it, which is rejection ABC at a 10% acceptance rate:

```{python}
epsilon = float(study.distance(study.reference).quantile(0.1))
print(f"ε = {epsilon:.3f} (z-score units)")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-comparison
#| fig-cap: "Comparing the prior simulations with S_obs. (4) Each prior simulation's mean and CV, in measured units; blue points are within ε of S_obs and accepted. The region within ε is an ellipse because each statistic's difference is divided by its own prior SD. (5) The same points as z-scores, where that region is a circle of radius ε. The line shows one rejected simulation's distance from S_obs."
case.plot_comparison(study, epsilon)
```

Both panels show the same 200 simulations and the same acceptances; only the
axes differ.

## What the Likelihood Approximation Compares

This page has so far covered the first of the three steps in @hartig2011,
aggregation (see the [overview](index.qmd#three-steps)). The second, the
**likelihood approximation**, is what makes inference possible for a stochastic
model. The likelihood $p(S_\text{obs} \mid \theta)$ can't be written down, but
the model can be run many times at any $\theta$, and the spread of the simulated
statistics shows how likely $S_\text{obs}$ is there. ABC turns those simulations
into a likelihood nonparametrically, by counting the share that land within
$\varepsilon$ of $S_\text{obs}$ (option (a) in @hartig2011). The parametric
alternative, option (b), fits a distribution to them instead, as synthetic
likelihood does with a normal distribution [@wood2010]. The third step,
sampling, decides which $\theta$ to simulate at; that is the job of the
algorithms on the method pages.

ABC methods never show the second step on its own. They run one simulation per
proposed $\theta$ and leave the averaging to the sampling. To see the step, we
hold $\theta$ at the truth and run 50 replicates there, as one job with its own
seed (`seed=2`). Each replicate is surveyed twice: without measurement error
(the surveyed cells' true heights, so model noise only) and with it (their
measured heights).

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
case.show_source(case.replicate_study)
```

```{python}
replicates = case.replicate_study(registry, cli, n=50)
replicates["distance"] = study.distance(replicates)

spread = replicates.groupby("observation")[case.STATISTICS].std() / pd.Series(study.scale)[case.STATISTICS]
spread.rename(columns=case.LABELS).round(4)
```

```{python}
replicates.groupby("observation")["distance"].describe()[["50%", "max"]].round(4)
```

The first table gives each statistic's spread between replicates, in prior SDs
(z-score units); the second, how far the replicates land from $S_\text{obs}$.

```{python}
#| label: fig-replicates
#| fig-cap: "Fifty replicate simulations at the true parameters, surveyed without (model only) and with measurement error, in z-score units. Left and centre: offsets from the pseudo-observed statistics (dashed), which are themselves one draw with measurement error. Right: the fraction of replicates within ε of the pseudo-observed statistics, the nonparametric estimate of the ABC likelihood at the truth, against ε; the dashed line marks the 10% rejection tolerance."
case.plot_replicates(study, replicates, epsilon)
```

The fraction of replicates within $\varepsilon$ estimates the ABC likelihood at
the truth for that tolerance (an indicator kernel). An ABC method estimates the
same quantity at every $\theta$ it proposes, with a single simulation each, and
its sampling algorithm combines those single draws into a posterior.

Two things follow from the figure:

- **The survey's measurement error is the larger noise source.** Model noise
  averages out over the 10 trees in each cell, so it barely moves the survey
  statistics; the measurement error on 8 cells moves them much more. The
  pseudo-observed data are one draw from the orange distributions, not their
  centre.
- **The tolerance decides what the posterior's width means.** Where
  $\varepsilon$ is far above the replicate distances, every replicate counts as
  a match, the likelihood at the truth is close to 1, and the posterior's width
  reflects the tolerance rather than the data's noise. The width starts to
  reflect the survey's noise only once a search tightens $\varepsilon$ toward
  the replicate distances, which is what the [SMC-ABC page](smc-abc.qmd)'s simulation budget
  has to buy.

## Starting a Method Page

Everything above is stored in the registry. A method page starts from the
middle with one call, which reuses these runs instead of re-simulating:

```{python}
#| eval: false
import forevertree_case as case

study = case.known_truth_study().load(registry, cli)  # survey, prior simulations, z-scores
result, session_id = study.search(registry, cli, "smcabc", settings, "forevertree_smcabc")
study.posterior(result)  # posterior mean and 90% interval, against the truth
```

For building an `SbiStrategy` by hand, `study.abc_target()` returns the z-scored
summaries function and $S_\text{obs}$.

```{python}
registry.close()  # the registry stays on disk for the other Inference pages
```
